query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled thermo‐mechanical treatment—specifically hot rolling (approximately 50% reduction) followed by rapid annealing (around 850°C for 30–50 seconds)—to HfZrTiTa0.53 will induce a dual heterogeneous microstructure (refined, recrystallized grains alongside retained substructures) that enhances room-temperature tensile ductility and uniform elongation without compromising its high yield strength or impact-triggered energy release performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 with reported metrics of ~786 MPa yield strength, ~1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain, demonstrating good strength and energetic potential but limited tensile ductility.
generation.intervention: Implement a thermo-mechanical processing route consisting of ~50% hot rolling followed by rapid annealing at approximately 850°C for 30–50 seconds.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static strain rates (∼10^–3 s^–1), with complementary compression and impact tests to assess load-bearing reliability and energy release.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual heterogeneous microstructure featuring a mix of fine, recrystallized grains and preserved deformation substructures, which together facilitate strain partitioning and promote deformation twinning.
generation.mechanism: The refined grain structure increases the density of grain boundaries and interfaces that act as barriers to crack initiation and propagation, while enhancing dislocation mobility and twinning. This synergistic effect improves uniform elongation during tensile loading and maintains high yield strength. Additionally, the preserved substructures support the rapid energy release on impact.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in room-temperature tensile uniform elongation (targeting >20% compared to the baseline 13.5%) with a yield strength reduction limited to less than 10%, concurrently preserving the impact-triggered energy release characteristics observed in the original alloy.
generation.baseline: HfZrTiTa0.53 reported to have 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain in its as-cast condition.
generation.boundary: The intervention must avoid excessive annealing that could over-coarsen grains or dissolve strengthening precipitates. The processing parameters are constrained to conditions that do not significantly reduce high-temperature strength or alter the impact energy release behavior, and the improvements are expected under room-temperature tensile conditions with quasi-static strain rates.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal rolling reduction percentage, annealing temperature, and time require further fine-tuning. The precise quantitative improvements in tensile ductility are uncertain and need validation, and there is a risk that modifications might inadvertently reduce the impact energy release capability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 samples: one set in the as-cast state and another set processed by hot rolling (~50% reduction) followed by rapid annealing at ~850°C for 30–50 seconds. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests at a quasi-static strain rate (~10^–3 s^–1) and perform complementary compression and impact tests. Use microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) to verify the formation of a dual heterogeneous structure.
measurements: Tensile uniform elongation (%) and yield strength from tensile tests
Impact energy release via standardized impact testing
Grain size distribution and presence of dual heterogeneity via microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanically processed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in tensile uniform elongation (e.g., an increase to at least ~20%) or if the yield strength decreases by more than 10% relative to the baseline, or if the impact-triggered energy release is adversely affected, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

High-Temperature Mechanical Properties of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). Enhancing the Strength and Ductility Synergy of Lightweight Ti-Rich Medium-Entropy Alloys through Ni Microalloying

Abstract: AbstractMedium-entropy alloys (MEAs) have attracted considerable attention in recent decades due to their exceptional material properties and design flexibility. In this study, lightweight and non-equiatomic MEAs with low density (~5 g/cm3), high strength (yield strength: 1200 MPa), and high ductility (plastic deformation: ≧10%) were explored. We fine-tuned a previously developed Ti-rich MEA by microalloying it with small amounts of Ni (reducing the atomic radius and increasing the elastic modulus) through solid solution strengthening to achieve a series of MEAs with enhanced mechanical properties. Among the prepared MEAs, Ti65Ni1 and Ti65Ni3 exhibited optimal properties in terms of the balance between strength and ductility. Furthermore, the Ti65Ni3 MEA was subjected to thermo-mechanical treatment (TMT) followed by cold rolling 70% (CR70) and cold rolling 85% (CR85). Dual heterogeneous structures lead to ultrahigh strength and uniform ductility in a Co-Cr-Ni medium-entropy alloy

Abstract: Alloys with ultra-high strength and sufficient ductility are highly desired for modern engineering applications but difficult to develop. Here we report that, by a careful controlling alloy composition, thermomechanical process, and microstructural feature, a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a dual heterogeneous structure of both matrix and precipitates can be designed to provide an ultra-high tensile strength of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation of 13% at ambient temperature, properties that are much improved over their counterparts without the heterogeneous structure. Electron microscopy characterizations reveal that the dual heterogeneous structures are composed of a heterogeneous matrix with both coarse grains (10∼30 μm) and ultra-fine grains (0.5∼2 μm), together with heterogeneous L12-structured nanoprecipitates ranging from several to hundreds of nanometers.
